name: Protect Democracy: defending US democracy (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US's people, whose government the work defends; the spillover abroad (a side-effect share of the US value) isn't assigned to countries.
summary: Protect Democracy litigates, builds tools and coalitions and writes policy to keep the United States from sliding into a more authoritarian government ($34.4 million in 2024). Its year of work is counted as its share of the money behind the US pro-democracy field's work against backsliding (about 1.3%) times the share of the forecast chance of the US leaving the democracies before 2030 (about 11%) that a year of the field's work removes (judged 4.5%); the loss is the income democracy brings (Acemoglu et al. 2019), building over 25 years, put off by the years a win counts and lasting until the slide would be undone (5% a year), and democracy's other goods. A smaller branch counts its work for proportional representation (about a twelfth of the result). With its next dollar at 35% of the average that comes to about 0.02 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, about a quarter of the site's global-health median. The result is mostly uncertainty, its own ranges spanning over ten thousandfold; the biggest is the field's effect on that chance, a judgment with no study behind it. Both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome

source.note: $28,277,727, including grants of $7,218,161; one programme described (monitoring, investigating, advocacy, lobbying, public outreach and litigation).

rows.explainer: Everything Protect Democracy Project, the 501(c)(3), spent on its programme in 2024, the latest year with a filed return (the audited statements, which the return says exist, aren't public). Its sister 501(c)(4), Protect Democracy United ($5,532,325 of expenses in 2024, its own Form 990, Part I line 18: https://protectdemocracy.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/FY24-990-PDU-Public-Disclosure-Copy-without-Schedule-B.pdf), is a separate organisation and not in this cost.

rows.label: Total expenses, calendar 2024
rows.explainer: The shared figure from the same return ($34,368,875, Part I line 18), read by the FairVote model too, which divides credit for proportional representation by Protect Democracy's spending.

rows.label: Spending on the modelled programme, calendar 2024
rows.explainer: The whole programme: the return lists one programme, and this model covers all of it, as two branches (defending democracy against backsliding; electoral-system reform). Grants to other organisations ($7.2 million, $5.5 million of it to Amalgamated Charitable Foundation, Schedule I) count as the work they fund, judged to be the same mix as Protect Democracy's own.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over the programme in proportion to its cost.

rows.label: Cost of the modelled programme, including overhead
rows.explainer: The year's full cost, the base for the charity's share of the field below.

rows.label: People governed by the US democracy the work defends (2024)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the United States: a slide into a hybrid regime would change how all of them are governed. The chance of that slide and the share of it the work removes are in p_success.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention in the year
rows.explainer: 0: Protect Democracy does no criminal or immigration casework; its cases are about elections, executive power and the people who run elections.

rows.label: Share of the programme spent on proportional representation
rows.explainer: The shared figure (7%, 3% to 15%), read by the FairVote model too: Protect Democracy lists four areas of work (Protecting Free & Fair Elections; Stopping the Consolidation of Power; Building Pro-Democracy Collective Action; Shaping the Democracy of Tomorrow, its own page); the last includes its work for proportional representation (research, a Democracy Journal symposium with Democracy Fund, a grant to Fix Our House) and its AI for Democracy Action Lab, which is counted in the backsliding branch; the return gives no split. The rest is the backsliding branch.

rows.label: Share of the programme spent defending against backsliding
rows.explainer: Litigation (election subversion, defamation suits for election workers, executive overreach), election protection (VoteShield, the National Task Force on Election Crises, the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections), state laws for election officials, the Civil Service Archive and OpenOMB, the AI for Democracy Action Lab, and public education: all aimed at keeping the US from sliding into a more authoritarian government.

rows.label: Chance the US stops being a democracy before 2030
rows.explainer: The shared forecast (about 11%): the stake the backsliding work acts on.

rows.label: Share of that chance a year of the US pro-democracy field's work removes
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Chance of backsliding removed by a year of the field's work
rows.explainer: The forecast chance times the share the field removes; Protect Democracy's part of it is its share of the field's resources (bs_attribution_share).

rows.label: Years until most of democracy's income effect is realized
rows.explainer: The shared figure (about 25 years, 20 to 30): the income effect of a change in how a country is governed builds up over this long.

rows.label: Income kept per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: A slide out of democracy averted keeps the income gain a democracy brings in the long run (about 21%, Acemoglu et al. 2019); the build-up is in bs_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the year's work until the slide it helps avert would have happened
rows.explainer: The forecast counts the Economist's reports published before 2030; those for 2024 and 2025 showed no slide, so the window left covers 2026 to 2028, and a slide averted would on average have come in its middle, 2027: three years after 2024's work (2 to 5). Not the same figure as the Brennan Center model's dem_years_until_effect (2.5, 1.5 to 4.5): that model's work year is the year to June 2025, half a year closer to the same date, so the two are one date measured from two work years, not two views of it.

rows.label: Discount for the wait (backsliding branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9): a slide averted counts as put off by these years, as a won reform counts as brought forward by them.

rows.label: Chance per year that a slide, once it has happened, is undone
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/democracy.json), read by every model of work against a US slide.

rows.label: Discount rate plus reversal hazard (backsliding branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the chance a slide is undone each year: the loss averted lasts only while the slide would have lasted.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years an averted slide counts (the loss ramp put off)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + bs_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + bs_rate) * ln(1 + bs_rate) * ramp_years) * bs_wait_discount
rows.explainer: A slide's income loss builds evenly over ramp_years from when it happens; putting the slide off by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp later, so the loss avoided each year is the ramp now minus the ramp years_of_impact later: it rises to a fifth of the full loss (5 of 25 years) over the first five years, stays there until the ramp is complete and falls back to nothing five years later, years_of_impact full-effect years in all before discounting. This is its present value (continuous form) at the shared rate plus the chance the slide would be undone (bs_rate), times the wait (at the shared rate): at the defaults about 1.5 full-effect years (5 undiscounted). Whether the slide comes later anyway is the question years_of_impact answers; how long it would last is bs_reversal_rate's.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the field's work (backsliding branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Everyone in the US × the long-run income kept × the shared value of a log point × the chance removed × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: People newly governed under proportional representation per year of the movement's work (2016-2025)
rows.explainer: The shared figure, read by the FairVote model too: the movement's 2016-2025 record, about 103,000 people a year (85,000 to 115,000), Portland, Oregon's 2022 reform most of it.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a switch to proportional representation brings
rows.explainer: The shared figure (5%, 1% to 15%), read by the FairVote model too: a reform within a democracy gets a ranged share of the democratization gain, never the whole (the family's rule); no study finds a robust income effect of proportional representation in rich democracies.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The reform's share of the long-run democratization gain; the build-up is in ref_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the win until the new system is first used
rows.explainer: The shared figure: two years (1 to 4), as in Portland (voted November 2022, first used November 2024).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (reform branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the shared yearly chance a won electoral reform is repealed (@democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate, 3%): repeal is a separate question from the years counted (the family's rule).

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won reform counts (its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + ref_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + ref_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + ref_rate) * ln(1 + ref_rate) * ramp_years) * ref_wait_discount
rows.explainer: As for the backsliding branch: the reform's effect builds over ramp_years from adoption, and bringing adoption forward by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp earlier; present value at the shared rate plus the repeal hazard, times the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the movement's work (reform branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly covered (already an expected count, so no separate chance) × the income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.explainer: The backsliding branch's figure, for reading: the main channel.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway, reform branch
rows.explainer: 1: the people covered are the movement's expected wins, and $win_years_counted already says they would have come some day.

rows.explainer: Institutional philanthropy for democracy (2021-2022) × the whole field's money against it × the direct share plus the rest at its relative effect, in 2024 prices: the field whose year of work the risk cut belongs to.

rows.label: Protect Democracy's share of the field's resources, backsliding branch
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on this work over the field's (Convention 2: share of resources, never an equal split): about 1.3%. It applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Protect Democracy's share of the proportional-representation movement's resources
rows.explainer: Its 2024 spending on this work (about $2.4 million) over the whole movement's average yearly spending in 2016-2025 (@democracy.us_pr_movement_resources_per_year, $3.4 million, its own and FairVote's included; Convention 2), the denominator the FairVote model divides by too: about 71%. A 2024 year of its work against an average movement year, so the result per dollar is the movement's wins per dollar it spent.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured, reform branch

rows.label: Side effect, reform branch: fairer elections valued beyond income, as a share of the income value
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a won voting-method reform (20%, 5% to 60%), read by the FairVote model too: below ue_freedom_wellbeing's 30%, which belongs to an averted slide, because a change of voting method within a democracy touches no basic freedoms.

rows.label: Side effect, reform branch: bans and counter-measures the win provokes
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a won voting-method reform (−10%, −30% to 0), read by the FairVote model too: state bans on ranked-choice voting close places to future reform.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not in the main chain, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The backsliding branch's two shared-form side effects (democracy's goods beyond income, backlash), each with its sign and weighted by the side-effects slider; bs_slide_side_factor adds that branch's slide-only two, and ref_side_factor swaps in the reform branch's own (the shared figures for a voting-method reform).

rows.label: Backsliding branch: its slide-only side effects, as a factor
rows.explainer: Repression averted and the pull of US democracy abroad belong to an averted slide, not to proportional representation: this factor adds them to the backsliding branch only, so with outcome_total's (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj) the branch counts 1 + all four side effects, the reform branch 1 + the other two.

rows.label: Reform branch: its own side effects, as a factor
rows.explainer: With outcome_total's (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj), the reform branch counts 1 + the shared side effects of a won voting-method reform (as the FairVote model does), not the averted slide's.
